s: is_in Boeotia Chaeronea was captured by Tolmides, the Athenian general. The Boeotians then surprised the Athenian forces there and won a bloody battle.

l: war between the Agrigentines and Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: War in Sicily between Agrigentines and Syracusans arose after Syracusans pardoned Deucetius; Siculi divided, armies fought at Himera, Syracusans won, and Agrigentines sought peace.

l: battle at the river Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Battle at the river Himera: Syracusans and Agrigentines camped opposite, fought, and Syracusans won, killing a thousand Agrigentines.

l: Thurium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Thurium was built in Italy near Thuria by an Athenian-led colony, after Apollo was declared founder following Delphi. Its compact plan had four lengthwise and three breadthwise streets. Conflict with ancient Sybarite inhabitants ended in their near destruction; Thurium became wealthy, allied with the Crotonians, and democratic.

l: Charondas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Charondas, a learned and accomplished citizen of Thurium, was chosen as legislator. He compiled laws from different countries and his own additions, addressing marriage, false accusations, harmful associations, education, orphans, military duty, and legal amendments. He died by his own sword after entering an assembly armed against his own law.

l: good laws of Charondas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The good laws of Charondas are a civic legal code emphasizing public education, military duty, household and office standards, guardianship, and strict obedience to written law. It punishes desertion, cowardice, false accusation, and association with wicked men, while regulating public office and orphans. Its culminating safeguard requires amendment proposers to wear a rope until a public vote, risking hanging if rejected, though some later changes passed.

l: laws of Zaleucus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The laws of Zaleuchus begin by attributing good to the gods, requiring purity in Locris, and valuing righteous action over costly sacrifice. They demand prompt reconciliation after animosity and condemn implacability as fierce and inhuman. They regulate magistrates against pride, domination, and biased judgment. They also restrain women’s attendants, nighttime walks, and luxury, while barring men from gold rings or Milesian garments unless marked by dishonorable guilt.

l: Thurium’s founding colony, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The founding colony of Thurium consisted of Sybarite exiles assisted by Athenians and other Greeks. The Athenians sent ten ships under Lampo and Xenocrates, while heralds invited people from the cities of Peloponnesus to join the colony. The colonists settled near the spring called Thuria and named their city Thurium.

l: Telys, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Telys, a political leader of Sybaris, gains great influence, incites scandals against wealthy citizens, persuades their banishment and confiscation, then demands Crotona surrender the exiles or face war.

l: the new Greek colonists, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: destroy the ancient Sybarite inhabitants [after becoming more powerful] The new Greek colonists at Thurium were initially disadvantaged by the ancient Sybarites, who reserved the chief magistracies, the first sacrificial honors for their wives, and the land nearest the city for themselves. Because the new colonists were more powerful, they eventually destroyed almost all the ancient inhabitants and took control of the city. They then invited additional people from Greece to cultivate and improve the rich country.

l: the Thurian citizens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_divided_into ten tribes [according to their countries of origin] The Thurian citizens became wealthy after inviting people from Greece to settle and cultivate the land. They divided themselves into ten tribes named according to their regions of origin and chose Charondas as their legislator. Their laws addressed family conduct, false accusation, harmful company, education, guardianship, military service, and the preservation of legal authority.

l: the Thurian democracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_governed_by the Thurian citizens [after the settlement and alliance with Crotonians] The Thurian democracy was established after the new colonists gained control of the city. Under it, the citizens were divided into ten tribes, and Charondas was appointed to organize their laws. The people also voted on proposed alterations to the laws, with the proposer risking execution if the change was rejected.

l: public education in writing, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: teaches writing [to all citizens' children] Charondas required all citizens’ children to learn writing, with the city paying the teachers’ wages. He considered writing especially important because it preserved votes, decrees, letters, wills, laws, knowledge, and the memory of the dead for future generations. The measure gave poor children access to instruction that their families could not otherwise afford.

l: Diocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Diocles is a Syracusan political leader, lawgiver, and chief among lawmakers, with great authority among the people. He advises revenge and punishment; after the Syracusans change their minds, his advice leads to executions and the imprisonment of Athenian citizens. He prescribes the Dioclean laws, opposes dishonesty, and finally kills himself to enforce his own law against entering court armed.

l: Zaleuchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Zaleuchus was born at Locris into a noble family, became a greatly learned scholar of Pythagoras, earned great esteem there, and was chosen by Locris inhabitants as their law-maker.

l: the inhabitants of Locris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: choose Zaleuchus [as their law-maker] The inhabitants were required by Zaleuchus's laws to believe fully in the gods, worship them, and keep their minds pure. They were also instructed not to remain implacable toward one another but to preserve the possibility of reconciliation and friendship with their adversaries.

l: magistrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Magistrates under the laws of Zaleuchus are commanded to avoid pride and domination and to judge impartially, uninfluenced by love or hatred.

l: women, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Free women of the city were regulated in public conduct: they could have no more than one servant abroad unless drunk, and were forbidden to go out at night or wear gold ornaments or gold-embroidered garments unless intending to play the whore.

l: Marcus Claudius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Marcus Claudius was identified as the fellow who claimed the young woman as his bondslave and obtained judgment against her before the Decemviri. He carried her away as a bondmaid after the corrupt judgment.

l: Lucius Valerius Potitus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Lucius Valerius Potitus, consul with Marcus Horatius, helped complete the Roman laws by adding the final two tables after the sedition.

l: Algidum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Algidum was the place where the army was encamped when the young woman's father came to report his calamity and seek assistance.

l: Aventine mount, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The soldiers entered Rome at night and took possession of the Aventine mount during their revolt against the Decemviri's conduct.

l: the patricians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: controls the power and authority of Rome [through monopolization] The patricians were said to have used their high birth and family glory to arrogate all the power and authority of Rome to themselves. The new arrangements were made as a check on their excessive power.

l: the common people, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: may_choose the consuls [both consuls, if they think fit] The common people were granted representation through ten tribunes of the people. The settlement also provided that one consul should be chosen from the common people, and that both consuls could be chosen from them if considered appropriate.

l: the Decemviri, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Decemviri are a body of ten law-makers who judge a young woman’s freedom claim. One corruptly makes her a bondslave; when soldiers revolt, they gather young men to defend him by force.

l: the twelve tables, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_made_of brass Ten of the twelve tables had already been completed when Marcus Horatius and Lucius Valerius Potitus became consuls. The two consuls added the remaining two, and the complete set was engraved on twelve brass tables.

l: the Roman laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Roman laws were completed after sedition with two final tables, engraved briefly and plainly on twelve brass tables, fixed before the court, and remained unto this day.

l: the laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The laws were made to check patrician power and protect common people, then publicly engraved on twelve brass tables before the court.

l: the great commotion at Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: ends Rome The great commotion at Rome ended when the parties agreed to establish ten tribunes of the people and alter the selection of consuls. The settlement brought the conflict to a close.

l: the sedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The sedition disrupted the laws being prepared by the Decemviri. After it, Marcus Horatius and Lucius Valerius Potitus completed the law code by adding two tables.

l: the soldiers' revolt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The soldiers' revolt began after the young woman's father reported her mistreatment and death to the army at Algidum. The soldiers entered Rome, seized the Aventine mount, and forced a settlement that expanded popular authority.

l: the young woman, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The young woman was a beautiful virgin of small fortune whom Marcus Claudius desired and tried to debauch. After a corrupt judgment declared her a bondslave, her father stabbed her to death to spare her the indignity and disgrace of that condition.

l: the young woman's father, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The young woman's father followed her after she had been carried away as a bondmaid. He stabbed her with a knife from a butcher's shop, fled Rome, and went to the army at Algidum to ask for assistance.

l: the army at Algidum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_located_at Algidum [encamped] The army at Algidum heard the young woman's father's account of his calamity and was moved by pity and sorrow. Its soldiers then entered Rome at night and took possession of the Aventine mount.

l: Samian revolt from Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a revolt [by the Samians against Athens] The Samians revolted from Athens because they perceived that Athens favored the Milesians in the dispute over Priene. Pericles suppressed the revolt, imposed an eighty-talent fine, and took hostages.

l: democracy in Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a democracy The Athenians set aside their democracy after their misfortunes in Sicily and transferred power to the four hundred. They later restored the democracy after Theramenes helped bring about the change.

l: Athenian-Samian war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a war [between the Athenians and the Samians] The Athenian-Samian war began with the Samian revolt and resumed after an aristocratic faction, aided by Persian soldiers, seized Samos. It ended when Pericles captured Samos, executed the revolt's leaders, imposed a payment of two hundred talents, took the ships, demolished the walls, and restored democracy.

l: sedition in Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a sedition [between democratic and aristocratic factions] A sedition divided Samos between supporters of democracy and supporters of an aristocracy. The anti-democratic faction obtained seven hundred soldiers from Pisuthnes, seized the city, expelled the opposing faction, and took back the hostages from Lemnos.

l: naval battle between Athens and Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a sea fight [won by Pericles over the Samians] Pericles defeated the Samians in a sea fight even though they had seventy ships and he had sixty. Later, when Pericles departed with part of his forces, the Samians attacked and routed the portion of his fleet left behind.

l: Phoenician fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_sent_by Persians [to aid the Samians] The Phoenician fleet was sent by the Persians to aid the Samians. Pericles left part of his forces besieging Samos and went to confront it, allowing the Samians to attack and rout the rest of his fleet.

l: siege of Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a siege [conducted by Pericles by sea and land] Pericles besieged Samos by sea and land after defeating the Samians in a naval battle. He used battering rams and scorpions, with the assistance of Artemon the Lacedaemonian, and continued assaults until the walls were breached.

l: fall of Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_caused_by Pericles [through assaults with battering rams and scorpions] Samos fell to Pericles after his engines battered down its walls. He executed the authors of the defection, required the Samians to pay two hundred talents, removed their ships, demolished their walls, and restored democracy.
